title: Daily X narrative digest — 2026-10-02

hits.name: Andrej Karpathy
hits.hook: Karpathy: stop reading LLM prose as the final artifact; ask for ASD-STE100, diagrams, HTML, or bespoke explainer videos.
hits.draft_en:
Karpathy's oversight post is the right altitude shift: as models do more legwork, your job becomes understanding outputs, not generating the first draft.

The practical ladder he lists is usable today:
1. ASD-STE100 (or ~80% STE) for constrained, readable explanations
2. Diagrams instead of walls of text
3. HTML apps you can click through once, then discard
4. Custom explainer videos (3b1b-style + narration API) as the format he is most bullish on

I already treat discardable software artifacts as cheaper than rereading a 2k-word answer. The test for agent builders: can your harness emit a one-shot explainer the human can verify in under two minutes? If not, you are still stuck in chat scroll.
hits.video_tip: Flash the STE100 blueprint image 6s (document structure / verb forms / sentence limits), then notepad: STE / Diagram / HTML / Explainer video. Caption: Oversight needs better artifacts. 30 seconds.
hits.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

hits.name: Andrej Karpathy
hits.hook: Karpathy on the Land-or-Water lat/long eval: models know geography from compressing the internet; plot 16,200 answers as a map.
hits.draft_en:
Karpathy calling the Land-or-Water coordinate quiz a cool eval is correct. Sixteen thousand text-only lat/long probes plotted as an image is a clean probe of compressed world knowledge, not tool use.

Builder takeaway: keep a few dumb, high-volume spatial or factual probes in your eval suite. They catch silent world-model regressions that coding benches miss. Do not confuse "the model knows land vs water" with "the agent can navigate a booking flow." Different failure modes.

If you ship agents that reason about places, run a cheap geo probe on every model swap before you celebrate the new leaderboard screenshot.
hits.video_tip: Show the Claude land/water map collage 8s if you can quote it, then talking-head 20s: Cheap geo probes catch silent regressions. Caption: World model != tool loop.
hits.text: Cool eval. Simply ask an LLM “Land or Water?” and give it a latitude and longitude coordinate as text. Ask 16,200 times, plot as image. The models know. From compressing the internet.
hits.original: Cool eval. Simply ask an LLM “Land or Water?” and give it a latitude and longitude coordinate as text. Ask 16,200 times, plot as image. The models know. From compressing the internet.

hits.name: Ethan Mollick
hits.hook: Mollick: frontier models now beat junior accountants on medium, well-defined tasks; 18 months ago they were well below.
hits.draft_en:
Ethan Mollick highlighting Mercor's accounting baseline is the career-compression chart of the week.

Medium-length, well-defined accounting tasks: models faster and more accurate than junior accountants, including the best in the study, after scoring well below humans 18 months ago. The companion cost chart puts Opus-class work around $0.21 per rubric criterion vs ~$10 for median accountant wage.

Practical response for agent builders in knowledge work:
- Separate "well-defined rubric tasks" from judgment, client trust, and exception handling
- Redesign junior roles around review, edge cases, and client context, not first-pass form fill
- Measure your own rubric, not theirs, before you cut headcount slides

The chart is real. The org design still has to be.
hits.video_tip: Show accuracy-vs-human scatter 7s, then cost-per-criterion bar (Opus ~$0.21 vs accountant ~$10 / 49x) 7s. Caption: Rubric tasks flipped; jobs did not auto-delete. 30 seconds.
hits.text:
“We find that on medium-length, well-defined accounting tasks, frontier AI models are now faster and more accurate than junior accountants, even the best one in our study.” Eighteen months ago they scored well below human accountants

Good discussion here: https://www.mercor.com/blog/human-baselines-for-benchmarks-ai-now-outperforms-junior-accountants/

hits.name: Philipp Schmid
hits.hook: philschmid: first time seeing unlimited human usage but capped agent / MCP tool calls on a pricing page.
hits.draft_en:
Philipp Schmid spotting "unlimited humans, limited agents" pricing is the packaging tell of the agent era.

The screenshot: Free = 100 MCP tool calls/week; Pro = 1M/week at $16/editor/mo yearly. Humans are cheap to seat. Agent tool loops are the scarce resource because they burn compute and create support risk.

If you sell or buy agent products, price and meter the tool loop, not the seat. And if you are building a harness, assume vendors will throttle agent usage first when they get scared. Design for graceful degradation when MCP quotas hit zero mid-job.
hits.video_tip: Flash Free vs Pro pricing (100 vs 1M MCP calls/week) 8s. Notepad: Meter the tool loop, not the seat. 25 seconds.
hits.text: My first time seeing unlimited human usage, but limit agent usage. Interesting.
hits.original: My first time seeing unlimited human usage, but limit agent usage. Interesting.

hits.name: Harrison Chase
hits.hook: Harrison: every agent harness needs a durable runtime; Pi Durable and LangGraph as the examples.
hits.draft_en:
Harrison's one-liner is load-bearing: every agent harness needs a durable runtime.

Pi ships Pi Durable; Deep Agents sit on LangGraph. Crash recovery, replay, and long-running state are not optional once agents leave the demo. If your loop dies when the laptop sleeps, you have a chat wrapper, not a harness.

Checklist before you call it production: checkpointed state, resume after failure, idempotent tool calls, and a clear owner for stuck runs.
hits.video_tip: Whiteboard 25s: Checkpoint / Resume / Idempotent tools / Stuck-run owner. Caption: Durable runtime or it is a demo.

hits.name: Ethan Mollick
hits.hook: Mollick: good AI made PowerPoints better for people who care; layouts, jokes, diagrams, not just default templates.
hits.draft_en:
Ethan Mollick's PowerPoint take is narrow and true: AI helps the people who already care about the talk, not the people who outsource thinking.

Same split shows up in agent demos. Teams that specify audience, claim, and evidence get better slides and better agent artifacts. Teams that prompt "make a deck" get prettier emptiness.

If you use agents for presentations, force a one-sentence thesis and three evidence bullets before any layout pass.
hits.video_tip: Talking-head 20s: Thesis first, layout second. Caption: AI amplifies taste; it does not create it.
hits.text: Sitting through PowerPoints has become much better since we got good AI. Sure, some people just let AI do the thinking work, but that is obvious (and they used default templates before). For people who do care, they have interesting layouts & funny visual jokes & good diagrams.
hits.original: Sitting through PowerPoints has become much better since we got good AI. Sure, some people just let AI do the thinking work, but that is obvious (and they used default templates before). For people who do care, they have interesting layouts & funny visual jokes & good diagrams.

hits.name: Jerry Liu
hits.hook: Jerry Liu: LlamaIndex Extract v2.5 agents claim SOTA price-performance vs Opus 5.5 / GPT-6 Sol on document extraction.
hits.draft_en:
Jerry's Extract v2.5 launch is the specialized-agent pattern: tune for value accuracy and grounding, publish ExtractBench numbers, ship citations with bounding boxes and layout-aware structural reasoning.

Reported lifts on long lists, cross-page records, and scanned forms, plus a claim of beating frontier generalists at 30% to 4x lower cost. Treat vendor benches as hypotheses. Re-run on your messiest PDFs, especially handwritten and multi-column scans, before you swap the pipeline.

If extraction is core to your agent, a specialist with grounded citations usually beats bolting another general model onto regex.
hits.video_tip: Flash LlamaIndex video thumb 5s, then notepad: Re-run ExtractBench claims on YOUR worst PDFs. Caption: Specialist + citations > generalist vibes. 30 seconds. Media is a talking-head product video; listen before quoting numbers live.

hits.name: Harrison Chase
hits.hook: Harrison on model routing done in the harness: understand tasks and models, build the router, track outcomes; ~64% median cost drop with no PR-quality hit.
hits.draft_en:
Harrison's routing post is the anti-vibes version of "just use the smart model."

Their numbers (Sep 16-22, 973 threads): Routed vs Always Astra cut median cost per thread 64% ($2.61 to $0.94) with merged-PR rate basically flat. The method: understand tasks, understand models, put the router in the harness, track outcomes.

Do not buy a magic router SaaS and hope. Instrument task types, log which model won, and keep the router where you already own retries and permissions.
hits.video_tip: Show Always-Astra vs Routed cost table 8s (median -64%, merged PR flat). Caption: Router lives in the harness. 25 seconds.

hits.name: jason
hits.hook: Jason: Dots burning 10 minutes on flight options is the same failure mode people already saw with coding agents.
hits.draft_en:
Jason's "they said this about coding too" quote on the Dots flight-booking rant is the latency-vs-autonomy trade in one jab.

If a human books a flight in two minutes, a ten-minute agent call that narrates Google Maps screenshots is not leverage. Same pattern as coding agents that thrash for twenty minutes on a five-minute fix.

Ship a fast path: agent proposes, human confirms in under a minute, or the agent stays quiet. Autonomy without a time budget is just a worse UI.

hits.name: Shreya Shankar
hits.hook: Shreya: per-row decision-model API calls are a terrible batch plan; SoL for one AI filter on 5k rows is ~6.6s on one H100.
hits.draft_en:
Shreya's SoL post should end naive "call Jev once per row" architectures.

With Qwen3-4B on one H100, speed-of-light for one AI filter over 5k movie reviews is about 6.6 seconds. No system today is close, including their Quail engine. Batch work needs query planning, KV reuse, selective filters first, and kernels that read shared prefixes once.

If your agent pipeline is thousands of independent HTTPS calls, you are leaving orders of magnitude on the table. Plan the job, do not just loop the SDK.
hits.video_tip: Notepad 30s: Per-row API = far from SoL / Plan batch / Reuse KV / Selective filter first. Caption: 6.6s SoL; your loop is slower.
hits.text:
Have you tried to use a decision model (like Jev) on thousands of rows? Calling an API once per row is a terrible idea for batch work, because it gets no benefit from query planning and sits *extremely* far from optimal performance.

With Qwen3-4B on one H100, the speed-of-light (SoL) for one AI filter over 5k movie reviews, or the fastest the GPU could possibly run it, is about...6.6 seconds! No system today comes close, including Quail, our open-source AI-SQL engine 😱

New blog post on how we cost AI-powered filters in Quail (based on SoL estimates), check it out! https://fsdatalab.github.io/blog/ai-filter-cost-estimates/

hits.name: Harrison Chase
hits.hook: Harrison: decision model season continues; Cloudflare open-weights Clef/Clef-flash join the class; swap decision models like main models.
hits.draft_en:
Harrison marking Cloudflare's Clef and Clef-flash as more open-weight decision-model entrants is the right harness note.

Decision models are cheap typed choosers for routing, approvals, and judging inside a loop. Your harness should swap them as easily as the main model. Locking routing logic to one vendor's Decisions API is how you inherit their calibration problems.

When you add Clef, Jev, Strands Decider, or Luna-decider, keep a held-out decision log and compare accuracy plus confidence calibration, not just latency blogs.

hits.name: Shreya Shankar
hits.hook: Shreya: bullish on workload-aware inference; declarative LLM pipelines should plan batches like databases do.
hits.draft_en:
Shreya connecting workload-aware inference to classic database planning is the systems post under the decision-model noise.

If you know the batch up front, reorder for KV sharing, run selective filters first, reuse document KV across ops, and pick attention kernels that read shared prefixes once from HBM. API-per-row throws that away.

Agent builders shipping document or eval pipelines: expose a declarative batch interface, not only a chat completion wrapper. Planning beats hoping the provider caches you.

virals.name: Shreya Shankar
virals.hook: Shreya on batch LLM pipelines: plan jobs, KV reuse, selective filters (self-quote under workload-aware inference).
virals.text: Yep! A batch data processing pipeline usually has several LLM operations, and the API approach makes one call per row per operation, with each call served independently. If you know all the requests up front, you can plan the whole job, like reordering requests within an operation to share KV cache, running the most selective filter first, and reusing each document's KV cache across operations. Also beyond planning, you also want to change execution — eg if you know which requests in a batch share a prefix, you can use different attention kernels that read the shared KV from HBM once, instead of once per request

outsiders.name: Shreya Shankar
outsiders.hook: Shreya on batch LLM pipelines: plan jobs, KV reuse, selective filters (self-quote under workload-aware inference).
outsiders.text: Yep! A batch data processing pipeline usually has several LLM operations, and the API approach makes one call per row per operation, with each call served independently. If you know all the requests up front, you can plan the whole job, like reordering requests within an operation to share KV cache, running the most selective filter first, and reusing each document's KV cache across operations. Also beyond planning, you also want to change execution — eg if you know which requests in a batch share a prefix, you can use different attention kernels that read the shared KV from HBM once, instead of once per request
outsiders.source: embedded quote via watchlist fxtwitter pull

The landscape has completely transformed since we started this a year ago. An exploding number of rogue agents, more breaches, more AI-driven attacks. now more than ever, security must be at the center of the AI conversation. With so much more hacks and vulnerabilities, this stuff is no longer theoretical...
reply_now.snippet: It's time to get serious about Security x AI.  One of the joys of doing AIE is helping others start their own high quality conferences in their countries and...
reply_now.reply_draft: Security x AI is the right conference theme once agents can buy, book, and post. The failure mode I keep hitting is not exotic jailbreaks; it is missing spend caps, tool allowlists, and identity on the agent acting for a user. If the summit talks stay at model-robustness slides and skip runtime controls, we will learn the hard way in prod.

reply_now.name: Hamel Husain
reply_now.text:
Q: Why do you recommend binary (pass/fail) evaluations instead of 1-5 ratings (Likert scales)?

A: Binary labels force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling, and involves significantly lower complexity to operationalize.

https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/why-do-you-recommend-binary-passfail-evaluations-instead-of-1-5-ratings-likert-scales.html
reply_now.snippet: Q: Why do you recommend binary (pass/fail) evaluations instead of 1-5 ratings (Likert scales)?  A: Binary labels force clearer thinking and more consistent l...
reply_now.reply_draft: Binary pass/fail is the part I had to relearn the hard way. Likert scores hid disagreement inside a polite 3. Splitting "accuracy" into separate yes/no checks for each required fact made labeling faster and error analysis actually actionable. I still only add numeric scores after the binary failure modes are stable.

reply_now.name: Andrej Karpathy
reply_now.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.
reply_now.snippet: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:  Writing. Something I've had success wi...
reply_now.reply_draft: The discardable-artifact ladder is what changed my day-to-day: STE-constrained prose, then a diagram, then a throwaway HTML explainer I can click once. Chat scrolls are a bad oversight UI. If the harness cannot emit something verifiable in under two minutes, I am still reading, not supervising.

reply_now.snippet: pretty clear every agent harness needs a durable runtime  pi :: pi-durable  deepagents :: langgraph
reply_now.reply_draft: Durable runtime is the line between demo and harness. Checkpointed state, resume after crash, idempotent tools, and an owner for stuck runs. If the loop dies when the laptop sleeps, it is not ready for always-on agents no matter how good the model card looks.

reply_now.name: Shreya Shankar
reply_now.text:
Have you tried to use a decision model (like Jev) on thousands of rows? Calling an API once per row is a terrible idea for batch work, because it gets no benefit from query planning and sits *extremely* far from optimal performance.

With Qwen3-4B on one H100, the speed-of-light (SoL) for one AI filter over 5k movie reviews, or the fastest the GPU could possibly run it, is about...6.6 seconds! No system today comes close, including Quail, our open-source AI-SQL engine 😱

New blog post on how we cost AI-powered filters in Quail (based on SoL estimates), check it out! https://fsdatalab.github.io/blog/ai-filter-cost-estimates/
reply_now.snippet: Have you tried to use a decision model (like Jev) on thousands of rows? Calling an API once per row is a terrible idea for batch work, because it gets no ben...
reply_now.reply_draft: The 6.6s SoL number should end per-row decision-model API loops for batch work. If you know the 5k rows up front, plan for KV reuse and selective filters instead of 5k HTTPS round trips. I have seen "simple SDK loops" become the real infra cost center.
